figures.caption: Figure 1: End-to-end pipeline of the SMILE framework. The pipeline performs a log-linear R2 scan to classify the problem into one of three cases: (C1) direct training, (C2) training on the inverted target, or (C3) decomposition into simpler subproblems. In all cases, the trained network is passed through a recovery pipeline consisting of greedy pruning, symbolic extraction, parametric optimization, and gradient-based coefficient rounding. HL denotes the number of hidden layers.
Figure 2: (a) Approximation of the Sigmoid function using a SMILE-based configuration. (b) Emulation of an L-layer MLP into an equivalent SMILE network using stacked SMILE layers and Sigmoid blocks.
Figure 3: Comparison of SMILE and baselines on the Feynman dataset in terms of SSR, accuracy solution rate (R2 > 0.999), and training time.
Figure 4: Pareto front of expression complexity versus accuracy on the Feynman dataset (right, accuracy solution rate) and the black-box dataset (left, median R2).
Figure 5: SSR on the Feynman and Strogatz datasets across all evaluated baselines.
Table 1: SMILE hyperparameters and pipeline configuration.
Figure 6: Comparison of all methods on the Feynman dataset in terms of median R2 test at multiple precision levels, expression complexity, and training time.
Table 3: Examples of expressions recovered by SMILE on the Feynman dataset under noise-free and noisy conditions.
Figure 7: Accuracy solution rate (R2 > 0.999) on the Feynman and Strogatz datasets across all evaluated methods.
Figure 8: SSR as a function of noise level for the top five methods on the Feynman and Strogatz benchmarks.

Figure 9: Ground-truth (left) and SMILE-recovered (right) expressions for six problems: three from the Jin et al. [38] benchmark and three from the Feynman benchmark. For three-variable problems, one variable is held fixed. Five expressions are recovered exactly (R2 = 1); the Gaussian PDF (bottom right) is a close approximation (R2 > 0.99).
Figure 10: Comparison of all methods on the black-box dataset in terms of median R2, expression complexity, and training time.
Figure 11: Ablation study on the Feynman dataset. Each configuration removes one pipeline component while keeping the rest unchanged. SSR, accuracy solution rate, and timeout error rate are reported.
